extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, juries, and patent litigators in U.S. patent infringement trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for determining damages (types, calculation start date, lost profits, reasonable royalty, apportionment, SEPs, evidentiary factors) and for assessing willful infringement in U.S. patent trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find that the accused device/method infringes any of the claims ... and that those claims are not invalid, you must determine the type and amount of damages to be awarded. The Plaintiff must prove each element of its damages—including the amount—by a preponderance of the evidence. Damages must be in an amount adequate to compensate the Plaintiff for the infringement and cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. You may not add anything to the amount of damages to punish an accused infringer or to set an example. You also may not add anything to the amount of damages for interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages aim to put the Plaintiff in about the same financial position it would have been in if the infringement had not happened. Do not consider damages unless you find one or more asserted claims both not invalid and infringed. 35 U.S.C. § 284; case citations included (WesternGeco; Bigelow; ResQNet.com; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Date Damages Begin — Alternate A (stipulated)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plaintiff and the Defendant agree that the date for the start of any damages calculation is [insert date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the stipulated start date when parties have agreed on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date Damages Begin — Alternate B (disputed — marking and notice rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The date that the Plaintiff first notified the Defendant of its claim for patent infringement is the date for the start of damages. The Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the Defendant was put on notice as of the date alleged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff can give notice to the public by marking substantially all products with the patent number or marking plus an Internet address linking product to patent number, or by direct specific notice to the Defendant. Marking is effective even if defendant did not see it. If Plaintiff did not provide effective public marking and did not provide direct notice before suit, Plaintiff can recover damages only after filing date (subject to Practice Note: if no products were sold or only method claims asserted, plaintiff may recover up to six years before filing). Relevant statutes: 35 U.S.C. §§ 286, 287(a); cases cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Damages Available
rubrics_metrics.description: Several kinds of damages are available for patent infringement, notably lost profits and a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits compensate what the patentee would have earned 'but for' the infringement. A reasonable royalty is the minimum amount of damages and is what someone wanting to use the patented invention would have agreed to pay just before infringement began. 35 U.S.C. § 284; cases cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits — 'But For' Test
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove lost profits, the Plaintiff must show by a preponderance of the evidence that, but for the Defendant's infringement, the Plaintiff would have made additional profits through the sale of all or a portion of the sales of the allegedly infringing products/methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must determine what purchasers would have done absent the infringement. The profits referred to are profits allegedly lost by the Plaintiff, not profits made by the Defendant. Case citations: Am. Seating; Aro; Ericsson; Tate Access Floors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits — Panduit Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff has proven lost profits if it proves each of the following by a preponderance of the evidence: (1) demand for the patented product/method in the relevant market; (2) absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes; (3) Plaintiff had the manufacturing and marketing ability to make all or part of the infringing sales; and (4) the amount of profit the Plaintiff would have made but for the Defendant's infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will explain each factor separately. Panduit Corp. v. Stahlin Bros. Fibre Works and subsequent Federal Circuit cases govern the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Demand for the Patented Product/Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand can be shown by significant sales of the Plaintiff's own patented product/method or demand for a product/method that directly competes with the Defendant's infringing product/method. Sales of Defendant's product can be used if the products/methods are sufficiently similar to compete in the same market or segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sales evidence to show market demand, but require similarity/competition to tie Defendant's sales to Plaintiff's product. Case citations: DePuy Spine; BIC Leisure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Acceptable Non-Infringing Substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether non-infringing acceptable substitutes competed with the Defendant's infringing product/method and what impact such substitutes would have had on the marketplace absent the Defendant's sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must have had advantages of the patented invention important to actual buyers, must be non-infringing (licensed or lacking required features), and must have been available during the damages period (need not have actually been sold; if not sold, Defendant must prove capability to produce it during period). If some customers would likely have bought substitutes, Plaintiff is not entitled to lost profits for those sales. Case citations provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Market Share (partial recovery when substitutes exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: If acceptable non-infringing substitutes existed, Plaintiff may still recover lost profits for a portion of Defendant's sales equal to Plaintiff's market share if Plaintiff shows it competed in the same market and would have made that portion of sales but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff need not prove only two suppliers; must prove market competition and entitlement by preponderance. Case citations: DePuy Spine; Ericsson; Crystal Semiconductor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Capacity (manufacturing and marketing ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must prove it had the manufacturing and marketing ability to supply the additional products/methods needed to make the sales it claims it lost, or that someone working with Plaintiff could have supplied them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also must prove ability to market and sell those additional outputs by a preponderance. Case citations: Wechsler; Fonar; Datascope; Gyromat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Amount of Profit (incremental income approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may calculate lost profits by calculating lost sales and subtracting any additional costs or expenses Plaintiff would have had to pay to make those lost sales. Amount cannot be speculative but need not be proven with unerring certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incremental income approach and legitimate cost adjustments. Case citations: Kalman; King Instrument; Paper Converting; Bio-Rad; Lam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price Erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff can recover additional damages if it shows that, but for Defendant's infringement, Plaintiff would have been able to charge higher prices or would not have had to lower its prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award equals difference between profits at the higher price and profits actually made at the lower price. If price erosion damages are found, the higher price may be used in calculating lost sales and lost profits, but must account for any decrease in Plaintiff's sales that might have occurred due to the higher price. Case citations: Siemens; Ericsson; Vulcan; Rite-Hite; BIC Leisure; Lam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost Escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff can recover additional damages if it proves by a preponderance that its costs (e.g., additional marketing costs) increased as a result of Defendant's infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must show costs went up because of Defendant's actions and not for some other reason. Case citations: Amstar; Lam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convoyed Sales (Collateral Products)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Plaintiff ordinarily sells its product along with other related collateral products, Plaintiff may seek damages for lost sales of collateral products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To recover lost profits for collateral products Plaintiff must prove (1) it would have sold the collateral products but for the infringement, and (2) the collateral products and the product/method are so closely related that they effectively act or are used together for a common purpose. Damages are calculated like lost profits for the primary product. Case citations: DePuy Spine; Rite-Hite; State Indus.; Paper Converting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: If Plaintiff has not proven lost profits (or proven lost profits only for part of the sales), then consider a reasonable royalty, which is typically calculated by applying a royalty rate to a royalty base. The reasonable royalty is the minimum amount of damages that a patent owner can receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable royalty must compensate for infringement and may be a lump sum or running royalty. Award must be based on the incremental value the patented invention adds to the end product and must reflect value attributable to infringing features and no more. Statute and cases cited (35 U.S.C. § 284; Power Integrations; Exmark; Ericsson; VirnetX; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Hypothetical Negotiation Method
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the royalty that would have resulted from a hypothetical license negotiation between Plaintiff and Defendant just before the infringement began, assuming the patent was valid and infringed and both parties were willing to enter into a license with full knowledge of the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume negotiation just before infringement; parties understood validity and infringement; may consider facts parties would have foreseen. Case citations: Aqua Shield; Apple v. Motorola; LaserDynamics; Uniloc; Fujifilm; Lucent; Maxwell; Rite-Hite; Wang Labs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Relevant Factors for Hypothetical Negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining reasonable royalty, jurors may consider evidence on any factors relevant to the economic value of the patent, including established royalties, comparable license rates, nature/scope of license, licensor policies, commercial relationship, promotional effect, duration/term, profitability/commercial success, utility/advantages over old modes, nature/embodiment of the invention, extent of Defendant's use, customary portion of profit for such use, portion of profit from patented invention vs unpatented features, expert opinion, and what the parties would have agreed upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List only those factors relevant and properly supported by evidence in the case. Specific factors enumerated in instruction (see guidance text) include (1) any royalties received by licensor, (2) rates paid by Defendant for comparable patents, (3) nature and scope of license, (4) licensor's exclusivity policy, (5) commercial relationship between licensor and licensee, (6) promotional effect and collateral sales, (7) duration/term, (8) established profitability/commercial success, (9) utility/advantages over old modes, (10) nature and commercial embodiment, (11) extent of Defendant's use, (12) customary portion of profit in business, (13) portion of profit from patented invention vs unpatented features, (14) opinion testimony of experts, (15) the amount licensor and licensee would have agreed upon, (16) any other economic factor a prudent business person would consider. Case citations provided (Ericsson; LaserDynamics; Wordtech; ResQNet; Monsanto; Maxwell; TWM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Attribution/Apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonable royalty must be based on the value attributable to the patented features, distinct from other unpatented features or other factors such as marketing or the Defendant's size or market position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The royalty base and rate must together reflect the value attributable to the patented technology. It is inappropriate to choose an unduly large base and then adjust by a lower rate, or vice versa; base must be closely tied to the invention. Case citations: Power Integrations; Exmark; AstraZeneca; Ericsson; Apple; VirnetX; Versata; Uniloc; ResQNet; Lucent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Entire Market Value Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalties generally should be based on the 'smallest salable unit' that practices the patented invention, not the entire multi-component product. If the smallest salable unit contains non-infringing features with no relation to the patented features, damages must be based only on the portion of that unit's value attributable to the patented technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entire Market Value Rule is a narrow exception: to base royalties on the entire product Plaintiff must prove the patented feature is the sole driver of customer demand or substantially creates the product's value. Estimation of a feature's value may be necessary even if never individually sold. Case citations: Ericsson; VirnetX; LaserDynamics; Uniloc; Lucent; Rite-Hite; Garretson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Multiple Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If Defendant infringed multiple patents, Plaintiff may be awarded separate royalties for each infringed patent and jurors may consider evidence about the number of patent licenses needed for the product and the effect on the hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cumulative license obligations when assessing hypothetical negotiation. Case citations: Ericsson; Apple; Verizon; Stickle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages are based on what the parties to the hypothetical license negotiation would have agreed upon at the time of the negotiation, not on hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence relevant to the negotiation is not necessarily limited to facts that occurred on or before the negotiation date; may include information parties would have foreseen such as usage after infringement started, subsequent license agreements, profits earned by infringer, and non-infringing alternatives. Case citations: Aqua Shield; Lucent; Studiengesellschaft; Sinclair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Availability of Non-Infringing Substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining a reasonable royalty jurors may consider the availability and cost of acceptable non-infringing substitutes to the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute is either licensed under the patent or does not infringe. Case citations: Prism Techs.; Mars; Zygo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Use of Comparable License Agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors may consider amounts other parties have paid for rights to the patents in question or for comparable technologies and the structures of such payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license need not be perfectly comparable, but if relied upon jurors should account for differences between those licenses and the hypothetical license (technology and economic circumstances). Case citations: Ericsson; Apple; LaserDynamics; ResQNet; Lucent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts Resolved Against Infringer (records rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts on the issue of damages due to the Defendant's failure to keep proper records should be decided in favor of the Plaintiff. Confusion or difficulties caused by the Defendant's records or lack of records should be held against the Defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This evidentiary allocation applies where defendant's recordkeeping deficiencies hinder accurate damages calculation. Case citations: Bigelow; Story Parchment; Minco; Sensonics; Lam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) — Practice Note
rubrics_metrics.description: For SEPs, Georgia-Pacific factors may be useful, but the jury must be instructed on the particulars of the FRAND commitment made by the patentee and on established patent law principles; only relevant Georgia-Pacific factors should be instructed. Any royalty award for a SEP must be based on apportionment of the incremental value of the portion of the claimed invention (or at least to the standard as a whole to which the patented technology relates). The royalty must be apportioned to the value added by standardization of the claimed invention, not the value of the standard as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not instruct juries on irrelevant Georgia-Pacific factors. Cite Federal Circuit decisions: CSIRO v. Cisco; Ericsson v. D-Link; Apple v. Motorola.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful Infringement — Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find that it is more likely than not that the Defendant infringed a valid claim of the Plaintiff's patent, either literally or under the doctrine of equivalents, then you must also determine whether or not the Defendant's infringement was willful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show willful infringement the Plaintiff must prove [text continues beyond chunk]; instruction establishes that willfulness determination follows a finding of infringement of a valid claim. (Further elements and burdens are in subsequent instruction text.)
